before.label: Political history
before.description: Examines institutions, diplomacy and struggles over power through different methods. Namier reconstructs parliamentary connections; Benson studies voters; Tilly investigates collective claims; Hunt joins political symbols and social identities. Hill, Dorothy Thompson and Flexner examine radical and rights politics, while Guha and Cooper investigate insurgency and labor under colonial rule. These approaches overlap without replacing all earlier political history.

Further contexts: Namier (1929), Flexner (1959), William Appleman Williams (1959), Hill (1972), Guha (1983), Tilly (1986) and Cooper (1996).

before.scope_note: Diplomatic, institutional, social, and cultural political histories persist and interact; the field did not disappear with the rise of social history. Distinguish institutional elites, electoral categories, popular organization and colonial subjects. Cultural political history can retain social and quantitative evidence; attention to popular action does not make all movements democratic. Regional examples are selective, not a globally complete political canon.

after.scope_note: Skinner’s interventions and Pocock’s political languages are related but not identical; the Cambridge School is narrower than all contextual interpretation. Public conventions constrain possible interventions; historical context is neither a complete causal deduction of a text nor recovery of a private intention without evidence. Later accounts dispute simple Laslett-to-Skinner founding narratives. Named philosophical resources are particular receptions, not school membership.

strands.title: Skinner’s philosophical resources
strands.focus: His retrospective account joins changing questions in Collingwood with language use in Wittgenstein and doing things with words in Austin. This records an acknowledged combination in Skinner’s work, not their doctrinal identity.

strands.title: Interventions, conventions and intended force
strands.focus: Skinner separates what words mean from what an author is doing with them. Public conventions and evidence constrain interpretation; a social setting alone does not determine the complete meaning of an intervention.
strands.works: Meaning and Understanding (1969), pp. 35–53

strands.title: Historically available levels of argument
strands.focus: Pocock asks at what level people actually formulated political ideas. A maximally coherent philosophical reconstruction and a history of thinking are legitimate but different inquiries; ideas remain historical events even when not the sole cause of action.
strands.works: The history of political thought: a methodological inquiry (1962), reprint pp. 3–11

strands.title: Republican fragility, virtue and corruption
strands.focus: Pocock’s introduction selects the problem of a republic’s existence in time, then proposes English and Atlantic continuations involving property, arms and commerce. It acknowledges Baron’s controversial resource and Skinner’s collaboration; this is a selected argument, not an exhaustive Atlantic narrative.
strands.works: The Machiavellian Moment (1975), introduction vii–x

strands.title: Philosophical precision and historical acts
strands.focus: Dunn distinguishes a proposition’s logical identity from a historical statement’s activity, including irony and polemic. Reconstructing the act requires evidence of the person’s available situation; philosophical and historical problems cannot simply replace one another.
strands.works: The Identity of the History of Ideas (1968), selected pp. 85–104

strands.title: Critical editions and disputed methodological succession
strands.focus: Laslett’s Locke edition and discussions with Dunn belong to contextual inquiry. They do not establish that Skinner inherited a complete method from him; Furuta’s later argument explicitly contests such a simple sequence.
strands.works: Two Treatises of Government, Laslett edition (1960); Dunn (1968); Furuta (2021), abstract

strands.title: Rights across philosophical and political contexts
strands.focus: Tuck traces natural-rights theories, Brett differentiates scholastic uses of ius, and Tully joins historical with critical inquiry around Locke. These projects extend the range of questions without forming one origin story; the present selections rely on scoped descriptions.
strands.works: Natural Rights Theories (1979); Locke in Contexts (1993); Liberty, Right and Nature (1997)

before.label: Conceptual history / Begriffsgeschichte
before.description: Traces changing political and social concepts in relation to historical experience, conflict, and expectations. Koselleck links conceptual change to different temporalities and to the emergence of modern historical consciousness. This overlaps with contextual intellectual history while asking different questions about semantic change across time.

after.label: Conceptual history / Begriffsgeschichte

Koselleck links conceptual change to different temporalities and to the emergence of modern historical consciousness. This overlaps with contextual intellectual history while asking different questions about semantic change across time. Collective German lexicon work, French studies of polemical usages and Richter’s comparisons represent distinct programs. Concepts can register and help shape social processes without exhausting those processes.
after.representative_figures_and_works: Reinhart Koselleck, Vergangene Zukunft (1979), translated as Futures Past (1985; Columbia edition 2004). The German conceptual-history tradition is related to, but not a branch of, Skinner and Pocock’s Cambridge School.

after.scope_note: Koselleck’s conceptual change and historical time differ from reconstructing a particular author’s intervention. Brunner, Conze and Koselleck’s editorial association does not imply identical methods or political commitments. Experience and expectation are formal research categories with variable contents; the proposed modern temporal transformation is neither a universal timetable nor a prediction of particular events.

strands.title: Words, concepts and overlapping semantic layers
strands.focus: The same word can persist while conceptual content changes; a concept can carry multiple historical layers. Koselleck combines synchronic usage with diachronic comparison without treating every word as a key historical concept.
strands.works: Futures Past, chapter 5, pp. 75–92

strands.title: Concepts as indicators and factors
strands.focus: Concepts register social relations and can help act upon them, but social events are not identical with their linguistic conceptualization. Historians must also distinguish actors’ terms from their own justified analytical categories.
strands.works: Futures Past, chapter 5, pp. 75–92

strands.title: Experience, expectation and unequal temporalities
strands.focus: These formal categories direct questions about remembered pasts and anticipated futures. Their asymmetry does not independently predict contents; Koselleck’s modernity thesis recognizes simplification, unequal social temporalities and recurring structures.
strands.works: Futures Past, preface and selected chapter 14 pp. 255–264, 271–275

strands.title: Collective lexicon, distinct programs and political criticism
strands.focus: Brunner, Conze and Koselleck participate in one editorial project with different research emphases. Criticism of Brunner’s political framing and textual revisions must be attributed and assessed through evidence, without assigning a uniform position to all editors and contributors.
strands.works: Geschichtliche Grundbegriffe; Koselleck’s preface and Tribe’s selected introduction

strands.title: French social roles and opposing uses
strands.focus: Gumbrecht and Reichardt investigate philosophe as a social role. Opponents can use similar semantic contents with opposed force; dictionaries participate in polemics instead of neutrally settling every usage. Their court discussion explicitly draws on Elias.
strands.works: Philosophe, Philosophie, Handbuch Heft 3 (1985), pp. 7–14

strands.title: Comparing conceptual history and political languages
strands.focus: Richter’s 1995 comparison makes differences among the German lexicon, French Handbuch and Skinner/Pocock programs explicit. Shared historical vocabulary questions do not establish one method or an origin of one school in another.
strands.works: The History of Political and Social Concepts (1995), chapters 4 and 6, abstracts

context.people: Expanded the five-person roster to sixteen with Dunn, Laslett, Gombrich, Kuhn, Ryle, Oakeshott, Baron, Anscombe, Brett, Tully and Tuck. Roles distinguish historians, editorial collaborators and specifically documented conceptual resources; no roster membership becomes an influence edge. Three contextual/conceptual historians are also selected in political history without counting that neighbor as fully reviewed.
context.works_and_arguments: Filled Pocock’s original empty work selection from the 1962 methodological excerpt and complete 1975 introduction, with the 1957 title bibliographically corroborated. Read Skinner 1969 pp. 3–12 and 35–53, Dunn selected original pages including the Ryle discussion, and Pocock’s complete available methodological excerpt. Later rights works retain publisher-description limits instead of claiming whole-book reading.
context.internal_distinctions: Six new approaches distinguish interventions and intended force, actual levels of political thinking, republican fragility, Dunn’s historical acts, Laslett’s editing and disputed methodological succession, and different inquiries into rights. The prior philosophical-resources strand is preserved. Social context matters without determining every intended performance; the programs are not collapsed into one Cambridge doctrine.
context.incoming_connections: Added Kuhn’s particular methodological resource in Skinner/Dunn and Dunn’s explicit use of Ryle’s Plato’s Progress. Existing Collingwood and Wittgenstein influence links gain contemporary 1969 primary support alongside their scoped retrospective interview.
